title: Market update - November 20th, 2026
summary: Bitcoin rebounds towards USD 64k on Anthropic IPO optimism, but the Fed has not finished tightening. Read our latest view on rates, AI and the USD 60k to 90k range.
body_markdown:
## Bitcoin’s bounce meets a Fed that has not finished tightening


A bit of green is welcome after the last few weeks, although we would be cautious about declaring victory just yet. Bitcoin’s recovery towards US$64,000 looks largely tied to improving risk appetite around Anthropic’s IPO. The deal was heavily oversubscribed and priced above expectations, while results from the likes of Nvidia have also helped steady sentiment towards AI after a challenging few weeks. Investors clearly have not lost their appetite for the theme, although they have become rather less forgiving about valuations.


There has been plenty of discussion about AI drawing capital away from crypto, and there is probably something in that. But the relationship works both ways. The recent deterioration in AI sentiment has been damaging for Bitcoin as part of the wider risk trade, so a recovery there can also help crypto. What neither market escapes, however, is the Fed. Improving sentiment around an IPO does little to alter the cost of capital.


Wednesday’s FOMC minutes


1 were more hawkish than Warsh’s press conference had suggested. Almost all participants judged that further rate increases would likely be appropriate under their baseline outlooks. Most supported holding rates in October, but a few of them regarded the decision as a close call. A couple of participants said a move larger than 25bp (a quarter of a percentage point) could warrant consideration in December if inflation data disappointed. For now, 25bp remains the central case, with the more important issue increasingly whether further tightening follows in January and March.


The minutes also contained an interesting warning on AI itself, with the staff highlighting the rapid growth in AI-related debt, off-balance-sheet leases and circular financing arrangements, and the risk that losses could be amplified if investment returns disappoint. Most participants observed that much of this borrowing sits in complex and opaque structures. That is another reason we struggle to see the case for a 50bp move unless the inflation data deteriorate materially. There is already plenty of leverage sitting inside the most rate-sensitive part of the equity market.


Retail sales have not made the Fed’s job any easier. Headline sales rose only 0.2% in October, but excluding autos they increased 0.6%, while the control group, the core measure used in GDP calculations, also rose 0.6%.


2 September’s headline increase was unchanged at 0.8%. Consumers appear more selective rather than meaningfully weaker, which supports the case for another hike even if it does not justify an aggressive one.


We believe markets are becoming a little too pessimistic on inflation. Inflation is a lagging indicator: oil has fallen from roughly US$113 to around US$92 per barrel over the last couple of weeks, and that will eventually feed through. The more important question is whether the Fed gets ahead of that disinflation or waits for it to appear in the backward-looking data. History suggests the latter is more likely, and that is probably the larger risk for markets now.


Crypto sentiment remains poor. Long positions have been unwinding, liquidity is thin, and even the bid-ask spread on IBIT, BlackRock’s spot Bitcoin ETF, has widened to around 17 to 19bp, which is about as close to peak bearishness as market plumbing usually gets. Momentum indicators such as the relative strength index also show markets oversold at present, so it is worth being cautious about extrapolating the current weakness indefinitely.


Gold’s sharp fall adds another useful perspective. Bitcoin has held up relatively well by comparison, although it may simply be that gold is catching up after having run much harder earlier in the year. Either way, Bitcoin’s refusal to break materially lower despite hawkish rate expectations, weaker risk appetite and persistent outflows is notable.


There are increasingly bearish calls for Bitcoin to revisit US$40,000, usually based on applying the drawdowns of previous cycles to the current one. We believe this is too simplistic. Institutional ownership is much larger than in prior cycles and is providing a degree of structural support that simply was not present before.


US$60,000 therefore remains a very important psychological level. Our outlook still assumes Bitcoin spends much of the period trading between roughly US$60,000 and US$90,000. A decisive break in either direction probably requires a much more aggressive change in monetary policy or liquidity conditions than we are seeing today.


The AI relationship is slightly more complicated over the longer term. Technology equities have historically had a strong relationship with money supply because they are long-duration, rate-sensitive assets, and AI is very much part of that trade. Bitcoin is also sensitive to liquidity, although it often moves earlier. If the AI investment cycle eventually suffers a more serious leverage-driven correction, Bitcoin would probably be hit with it initially and may even lead the move. We would also expect it to recover faster once investors start distinguishing between a leveraged capex cycle and an asset whose monetary characteristics are rather different.


Waller’s speech this week was constructive in that respect. He described the convergence between blockchain and traditional finance as clearly under way, with tokenised stocks, bonds and commodities (issued as digital tokens on a blockchain) increasingly moving on-chain. Stablecoins, tokenised deposits and money-market funds could coexist with conventional payment rails, while traditional firms and decentralised finance (DeFi) businesses compete across multiple models. His caveats were around governance, custody and legal certainty rather than the direction of travel.


So sentiment has improved slightly, but the rates problem has not gone away. The market is probably too pessimistic on some parts of the inflation story and too optimistic about how quickly the Fed will acknowledge that. Until that tension resolves, Bitcoin looks more likely to grind around within its range than embark on a clean trend.

1


Federal Reserve, Minutes of the Federal Open Market Committee, 27 to 28 October 2026, published 18 November 2026


2 US Census Bureau, Advance Monthly Retail Trade Report, October 2026, released 17 November 2026
